<reason>Both sides argued competently, but B identified and sustained a genuine structural flaw in A's case that A never fully resolved. Once A conceded that its "Antarctic-like" treaty would only cover the central Arctic Ocean/Lomonosov Ridge and would not touch coastal sovereignty or demilitarize national territory, B repeatedly and correctly pointed out that A's own evidence of danger (Russian coastal base expansion, NATO responses near Kola/Alaska/Greenland) lies entirely outside that scoped treaty's jurisdiction. This "referee for the wrong game" critique, introduced in Rebuttal 1 and sharpened through the pressure questions and both closings, put A in a genuine bind: either widen the treaty to something unratifiable and expropriative, or narrow it to something that governs only low-stakes "prestige mud" while leaving the actually dangerous militarized coasts untouched. A's answer (A4.5) tried to blur this distinction by pointing to militarization "around" the contested waters, but B had already carefully separated coastal buildup from the high-seas pocket, and A's closing never directly re-engaged this mismatch, instead reasserting the "unresolved pocket" framing without explaining why that pocket's resolution matters more than the coastal military dynamics that supplied most of A's own urgency evidence. B also offered a plausible, if counterintuitive, mechanism (ambiguity avoids public losers, forced verdicts manufacture them) that A never fully dismantled. The result is a debate where B's rebuttals did more real damage to the opponent's live route to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's repeated separation of coastal militarization (real, but outside PRO's proposed treaty scope) from the "empty" central pocket the treaty would actually govern (B2.3, B4.1, B5.2) — a mismatch A conceded existed but never resolved.</best_rebuttal>
